analysis.title: Global Economics Daily Points, November 20, 2026
key_insights: The note says Anthropic's IPO, described as the biggest ever, rallied above its $83 issue price on the first morning, faded to a modest gain by the close, and is down sharply pre-market. Broader equities did not share the enthusiasm.

The note reads this as a sign of how durable the tech trade is. When SpaceX debuted in June it rallied for a few days alongside general risk-on sentiment, including tech. This time that did not happen. Chart 1 (Google Trends) shows more search interest in Grand Theft Auto VI than in Anthropic.
The S&P and Nasdaq each fell more than 2% yesterday. Futures point to a further 1-2% decline this morning, TSX futures are down just under 1%, and European cash markets are lower.

Safe-haven flows are going into sovereign bonds. Yields are down across the US, Canada and all of Europe. Gold is down another $60/oz. The dollar is not benefiting, since most major currencies are up against it.

Oil is slightly lower. The author expects Trump to defer talk on Iran until next month, guessing he does not want to antagonize the GOP during the lame duck session when he needs them for other things.
Canadian retail sales volumes rose only 0.1% m/m SA in September. Nominal sales rose 0.8% (0.7% initial guidance) and August was revised up to 1.4% from 1.2%.

Statistics Canada's preliminary October flash guidance for nominal retail sales was -1.5% m/m SA. Scotiabank's price tracking suggests lower volumes drove it, since CPI-gas rose 1.9% m/m SA in October.

Canadian real retail sales are tentatively tracking just shy of a -2% q/q SAAR contraction in Q4, after 3.9% q/q SAAR growth in the prior period shown in chart 2. The note says it is early, with the holiday season still ahead.

UK retail sales volumes ex-gasoline rose 0.9% m/m SA in October against 0.1% consensus. A downward revision to the starting point (-0.9% instead of -0.7%) gave only a partial assist. Momentum has been positive since 2024 but at a tepid pace.

Trump's noon ET press conference on his Asia trip is expected to reveal little. The note says there were no breakthroughs in talks with Putin and Xi, and nothing substantive agreed on Ukraine, Iran or US-China trade.

Canada's lead trade minister Dominic LeBlanc floated acceptance of some reduced level of US tariffs. He wants an interim deal with relief on Section 232 and Section 338 tariffs, ideally eliminating the latter and reducing the former, before any broader CUSMA renegotiation.
No firm timeline was set for a Canada-US deal, and negotiations may stretch into the new year. LeBlanc did not say what Canada would offer in retaliatory tariffs, investment or purchases of US goods.

The note sets out arguments on both sides of accepting an interim deal. The hold-firm side argues Canada should rely on US courts, Congress and voters, and that codifying tariff acceptance would be hard to unwind. The take-relief side argues all-or-nothing has no place in trade talks and that waiting is costly for affected sectors.

Chart 4: removing the Section 338 tariffs would cut the US effective tariff rate on Canadian goods by a little over three percentage points. Cutting the Section 232 auto and steel tariffs as well could bring the overall rate down to the low single digits.

The note calls the tariff issue a political calculus with concentrated significance for a handful of sectors but modest macroeconomic consequences. It adds that Canada has performed fine in the tariff era, Canadian borrowing costs are likely to stay below US costs, and US growth can keep pulling Canadian exports.

Central bank rates in the report's table are Fed 4.00%, BoC 2.50%, BoE 4.00%, ECB 2.65%, BoJ 1.25%. The Fed and BoC meet Dec 9, the RBA Dec 7, the RBNZ Dec 8, the BoE and ECB Dec 17, and the BoJ Dec 18.

tension_points.bull_case: Accept an interim deal to get relief on Section 232 and 338 tariffs, keep negotiating, and reduce pain for affected sectors. Removing the Section 338 tariffs would cut the effective tariff rate by a little over three points, and all-or-nothing has no place in trade negotiations.
tension_points.bear_case: Hold firm. Accepting any tariffs risks codifying them against the spirit of the trade deal. The US administration is weakened after the midterms, Canada can rely on US courts, Congress and voters, and any agreement may not be honoured.
